title: The temple dedicated (1 Kings 8:22–30)
hookLine: heaven can't contain you, how much less this house

cards: The house is finished. Cedar, stone, gold. The ark has been carried into the inner room, and a cloud has filled the house, so that, the text says, the priests could not stand to minister.

Now Solomon stands before the altar, in front of the whole congregation of Israel, and spreads his hands toward heaven. The work is done, and a crowd is waiting. A builder's speech would be easy here: look what we made.
What comes out of his mouth instead is a question that almost undoes the building.

teach.b: Here's the question, in the King James Bible: "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?"
He says it on opening day. Then what is the house for? Solomon answers in the next breath.
He doesn't ask God to move in.

teach.h: THINE EYES OPEN TOWARD THIS HOUSE.
teach.b: He asks God to look: "That thine eyes may be open toward this house night and day." And to listen.
When your people pray toward this place, "hear thou in heaven thy dwelling place: and when thou hearest, forgive." The hearing happens in heaven. The house is not a box for God.

teach.h: A DIRECTION TO TURN YOUR FACE.
teach.b: It's a direction, a place to turn your face.

As the prayer goes on, Solomon pictures people praying toward it from far away: a stranger from a distant country, his own people carried off into a foreign land, turning toward the city and the house.
Later, the book of Daniel shows a man in exile doing just that, praying with his windows open toward Jerusalem. Christians carry this prayer in more than one way.
Some hear an echo in John's Gospel: "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Others point to Paul, who tells a church, "ye are the temple of God."
And some carry Solomon's question into the churches they build: a house that can't hold God, opened anyway as a place to turn and pray.

how: Some churches hold a service of dedication when a new building opens, and Solomon's prayer in 1 Kings 8, with its admission that heaven cannot contain God, may be read there.

games.q: you're Solomon. the house is finished, the whole congregation is watching, and you spread your hands toward heaven. what do you say about the house?
o: here, at last, God will live among us.
will God indeed dwell on the earth? this house can't contain you.
look at the cedar and gold we gave.
games.why: on opening day he admits the house can't hold God, and asks instead that God's eyes be open toward it, and that God hear, and forgive.

practice: Bring to mind a place that's holy to you, or simply dear: a church, a grave, a grandmother's kitchen, a hill you used to climb. If you know which way it lies, turn toward it; if not, face a window.
If you pray, pray toward that place now, in silence or in your own words; if you don't, let it be the direction of your attention for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Solomon. The king who, on the day his temple opened, admitted heaven itself can't contain God, and asked only for open eyes and a listening ear toward it.

orig.note: Hebrew: house, the plain word Solomon uses for the temple: how much less this house (1 Kings 8:27).

carryVoice: Your line: heaven cannot contain you. Seven days, from Mephibosheth through Uriah and a father's grief, to a wise request, two mothers and a finished house. Day seven hundred twenty-eight, done.
